stocks.title: 2026/10/21(三)全台游資氾濫 為何會錢荒?股匯大矛盾!台幣越貶經濟越強？【早晨財經速解讀】
stocks.transcript_raw: Investors, welcome to Morning Financial  Interpretation. It is Wednesday,  October 21, 2026, 8:31 AM Taipei time.  Good morning everyone, I'm Hao. For  this half-hour session, we are here to  walk you through the shifts in global  financial news. The US stock market  shows mixed results; some positive  corporate earnings are emerging, and  oil prices are pulling back, though  they have stopped falling. There are  two angles we really need to watch. On  one hand, with earnings reports rolling  out, stocks aren't rising. Does this  mean P/E ratios are continuing to  decline? What level are we at now?  Secondly, let's look at Taiwan. The  depreciation of the New Taiwan Dollar  is a bit extreme this time, and selling  pressure from foreign investors is  quite heavy. How should we understand  an economy with 10%growth whose  currency is being sold off like this?  How do we interpret this major  contradiction in stocks and currency— the weaker the NTD, the stronger the  economy? On the other hand, we keep  talking about excess liquidity and how  ETF buying shouldn't be a concern, but  why is there a cash crunch? How can we  have both excess liquidity and a  shortage of cash at the same time?  Today, I'll share some observations  with our investor friends. Actually,  the US market seems to be attempting to  bottom out. Since big tech stocks— like those in the Nasdaq and S&P— haven't fallen yet, it represents a  degree of sector rotation from a market  cycle perspective, as big stocks  haven't softened yet. More importantly,  major stocks are now releasing their  earnings. If you observe closely, since  most stocks haven't hit new highs after  these reports, it results in a  continuous decline in P/E ratios. If we  look at the forward P/E ratio of the  Nasdaq for the next year, it has fallen  to 20.5 x. It was close to 25x at the  end of last year. What kind of level is  this 20.48 x? It’s already lower than  it was during the war earlier this year , roughly equivalent to the tariff war  levels of 2025, and has even returned  to the lows of the 2022 Russia-Ukraine  war. In other words, while it may not  be cheaper than the 2022 low, it is  roughly at its cheapest point in the  past four years. At this rate, once  this quarter's earnings are all  released, the P/E ratio could  potentially break through to 18 or 19  times. So, if we observe it from the  perspective of P/E valuation, it is  actually quite attractive. Of course,  some will factor in the high interest  rates in the bond market, arguing that  the higher the rates, the lower the P/E  should be, so a moderate mean reversion  is acceptable, as current benchmark  rates are indeed high relative to the  past 20 years. However, I think this is  a good reference indicator; at the very  least, it's not expensive, and you can  judge for yourself just how cheap it is . In fact, the Nasdaq 100 index has  returned to roughly the level it was at  around mid-September. The real pressure  point right now isn't actually about  liquidity risks or instability in these  large-cap tech stocks, but rather the  significant widening of credit spreads  in U.S. investment-grade bonds. If we  take a closer look at the CDS prices  for two major companies like Nvidia and  Broadcom, the speed of their increase  is incredibly fast. Looking at the 5- year credit default swap (CDS) spread,  it was about 35 to 40 basis points in  June, and by October it had......risen  to 98 to 144 basis points. The  insurance premium isn't exceptionally  expensive yet, but the point is that  the rate of increase is about three to  four times, hitting new highs for this  period in just six months. Broadcom's  credit hedging costs have increased by  about three times, yet the Nasdaq 100  index has only fallen by 5%, so why  hedge so much? This shows that a  certain group of people is clearly very  worried; they believe that since stock  prices haven't fallen yet, a catch-up  decline is highly likely, so they have  taken certain hedging measures in  advance. This is a direction we can  observe. If we look at the big picture,  regarding the overall North American  average investment-grade credit default  risk (CDX.IG), the spread has risen  from 50 basis points in September to  62.1 basis points now. This is a high —well, not an all-time high, as it  was higher during past financial crises , but it is a new high since March or  April of this year. So, while we don't  see a major impact overall, at the  individual stock level, there is a  sense that the credit market is  becoming more anxious than the stock  market. It seems quite a few people  believe that the index is not holding  up, and that it needs to catch up to  the downside; some people are saying  this, so we can monitor the situation  further.
